title: MB8-10695
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (the appellant), a citizen of Haiti, is appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated April 25, 2018.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the appellant), a citizen of Haiti, is appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated April 25, 2018. The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD's determination that the appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

The appellant was allegedly threatened by a group of individuals in XXXX 2012 when he was XXXX his grandfather's land. He explained that these individuals were armed and affiliated with authorities. The appellant states that on XXXX XXXX, 2012, he took refuge on the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, but found it impossible to live there, as he had no family or employment; moreover, he felt isolated and unsafe. Subsequently, the appellant allegedly left for Florida by boat and arrived there on XXXX XXXX, 2013. He made a claim for asylum in the United States on XXXX XXXX, 2017, but had not received a response as of the day of his hearing before the RPD. On XXXX XXXX, 2017, he left the United States for Canada, where he claimed refugee protection.

The RPD found that the claimant failed to establish that there is a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that, on a balance of probabilities, he would be personally subjected to a danger of torture or a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if he were to return to his country. The RPD also found that the appellant was not a credible witness in regard to several pieces of evidence, due to his many contradictions and omissions.

Lastly, the RPD found that the appellant was generally not credible due to the accumulation of contradictions and omissions. For his part, the appellant alleges that the RPD erred in its assessment of his credibility.
The RAD must apply the correctness standard to questions of fact, questions of mixed fact and law and questions of law, except in cases where the RAD has a meaningful advantage.1
paragraphs.heading_before: THE ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

paragraphs.text: I have conducted an independent analysis of all the evidence on the record, including a full review of the testimony given at the hearing, in order to form my own opinion on this refugee protection claim and determine whether the RPD's decision is correct. ANALYSIS a. Appellant's credibility

The claimant has the burden of establishing before the RPD that he has a well-founded fear of persecution or that, more likely than not, he will be personally subjected to a risk to his life, a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture, if he was to return to his country of citizenship. An important indicator of a witness' credibility is the consistency of his story.2
The RPD analyzed four categories of evidence on the record before addressing the issue of the appellant's credibility.

The first issue is who is the actual owner of the land in Haiti: does it belong to the appellant's father or grandfather? The RPD noted3 a contradiction between the appellant's testimony and the information provided in his Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form). The appellant explains in his memorandum4 that he corrected his error, which he had made during his testimony because he felt stressed at the time of the hearing.

For my part, I accept the appellant's explanation for this contradiction in fact, considering that this is his first time attending a hearing. On the other hand, having listened to the recording of the hearing, I believe that, more likely than not, the error occurred because of a minor interpretation issue.5
Thus, I conclude that the RPD's finding on this element is erroneous and I find that the appellant's credibility is not undermined.

Second, the RPD noted several conflicting dates in the appellant's testimony and his BOC Form, including the appendices,6 particularly the dates of the alleged conflict on his grandfather's land (XXXX 2013 or XXXX 2012) and the appellant's escape to the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (XXXX 2013 or XXXX 2012). When questioned by the RPD about these inconsistencies, the appellant noted that the errors were made by a woman who assisted him with his BOC Form; finally, the appellant acknowledged that there is a conflict. In his memorandum, the appellant argues that his story is perfectly consistent7 despite these errors. In short, the RPD did not accept the appellant's explanations to the effect that a woman helped him complete his BOC Form, and that she is to blame for the errors on the form.

In his memorandum8 and his BOC form,9 the appellant states that he left Haiti for Florida on XXXX XXXX, 2013. He even explains that he [translation] "left on that specific date"10 (emphasis added). Elsewhere in his BOC Form, he contradicts himself and indicates that he left Haiti for Florida by boat on XXXX XXXX, 2013.11 He testified at least four times that he left the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX on XXXX XXXX, 2013.12 His memorandum13 and his BOC Form14 show that he arrived in the United States on XXXX XXXX, 2013. Apart from the fact that the date of his departure from Haiti is not well established by the evidence on the record, there is also an error in one of the alleged timelines: the appellant could not have arrived in the United States (XXXX XXXX, 2013) before leaving Haiti (XXXX XXXX, 2013), as he claims he did.15

In response to this problematic timeline, the appellant asks to be given the benefit of the doubt as to the dates of these events, stating that he [translation] "becomes confused when asked to pinpoint these events on the calendar, as he does not have a good memory for dates."16

I do not accept the appellant's explanations for two reasons. First, as established above, there are quite a few inconsistencies and contradictions concerning dates in this case and they occur repeatedly in both the BOC Form and his memorandum, when they could have been corrected. More importantly, the main concern is the contradictions concerning the events surrounding the appellant's grandfather's death. In my opinion, while it is possible to forget the precise dates of a conflict or a move, a person would normally remember at least the sequence of these events concerning a major event such as a death of a loved one (i.e. the grandfather's death in this case).
Thus, I agree with the RPD that these inconsistencies undermine the appellant's credibility in this case, since they relate to central or important aspects of the refugee protection claim.

Third, the RPD questioned the appellant's failure to disclose an incident when he was threatened on the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX,17 noting that the burden of proof was on the appellant and such that his declaration in his BOC Form requires such disclosure. The appellant responded that he had thought of it when he filled out his BOC Form and no one questioned him about it.

Given that these very threats [translation] "that endangered his life"18 ultimately motivated the appellant to leave by boat and go to the United States (in other words, a major decision: [translation] "I did not want to die"19), I do not accept the appellant's explanations to the effect that he simply did not consider including them in his BOC Form. This omission is serious, given the consistency it adds to the applicant's written account.
I agree with the RPD that the appellant's failure to mention these allegations seriously undermines his credibility.

Fourth, the RPD noted a contradiction concerning the appellant's failure to seek help from the authorities.20 It also noted that the appellant could not remember the name of the group of criminals. In response, the appellant argues that the RPD conducted a microscopic examination21 of the evidence.

I agree with the appellant on this point. This might not be a contradiction, but rather a situation that occurred for various reasons. More precisely, it is possible that the appellant did not seek the assistance of Haitian authorities to protect himself from the criminals because the criminals are more heavily armed than the authorities and also because they are affiliated with the authorities. In other words, there could be more than one explanation for the appellant's behaviour in this regard.
Thus, I conclude that the RPD's finding on this element is erroneous and I find that the appellant's credibility is not undermined.

In the end, after considering all of the reasons for the RPD's decision, as well as the appellant's full testimony and his arguments in his memorandum, I conclude that the RPD finding that the appellant not credible is correct, because these findings of non-credibility, which I uphold, concern important information and relate to central elements of the refugee protection claim. I consider them to be significant enough to find the appellant not credible.

After considering all of the evidence on the record, I conclude that there is no serious possibility that the appellant would be persecuted in Haiti on a Convention ground, or that, on a balance of probabilities, he would be subjected to a danger or torture or a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if he were to return to his country of citizenship.

Consequently, the RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD's determination that the appellant, XXXX XXXX, is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.
